outputs.L3:
The device is a dual-pinion electric power steering system configured to turn a turnable member, such as a vehicle wheel, by moving a rack shaft. The rack shaft is provided with rack teeth and is arranged so that its movement is converted into turning motion of the turnable member.

The system includes a first pinion shaft that receives steering force transmitted from a steering wheel. The first pinion shaft meshes with first rack teeth formed on the rack shaft, so that rotation of the steering wheel is transmitted through the first pinion shaft to the rack shaft. As a result, the rack shaft moves in accordance with the driver’s steering operation.

The system also includes a second pinion shaft that receives rotational driving force from an assist motor. The second pinion shaft meshes with second rack teeth formed on the rack shaft. When the assist motor operates, its rotational force is transmitted through the second pinion shaft to the rack shaft, thereby assisting movement of the rack shaft and reducing the steering effort required from the driver.

To maintain proper meshing engagement, a first pressing member is provided to press the rack shaft toward the first pinion shaft. In addition, a second pressing member is provided to press the rack shaft toward the second pinion shaft. These pressing members help stabilize the engagement between the respective pinion shafts and rack teeth.

The first pressing member is configured to have lower rigidity than the second pressing member. Accordingly, the support characteristic at the steering-wheel-side pinion engagement portion is made more compliant than that at the assist-motor-side pinion engagement portion. This arrangement can help balance steering feel, suppress undesirable vibration or noise, and maintain reliable transmission of both manual steering force and motor assist force.
outputs.L4:
A dual-pinion electric power steering device is provided in which a rack shaft is arranged to move in an axial direction in response to steering operation. The rack shaft includes a first rack portion that meshes with a first pinion connected to a steering wheel through a steering shaft, and a second rack portion that meshes with a second pinion driven by an electric assist motor. Rotation of the steering wheel is transmitted mechanically to the first pinion, causing the rack shaft to move and steer the vehicle wheels. In addition, the assist motor applies an auxiliary steering force through the second pinion, thereby reducing the steering effort required from the driver.

The rack shaft is supported at two locations corresponding to the first and second pinions. At the first pinion side, a first pressing member is provided opposite the first pinion with the rack shaft positioned between them. The first pressing member urges the rack shaft toward the first pinion so that proper meshing between the first rack portion and the first pinion is maintained. At the second pinion side, a second pressing member is provided opposite the second pinion with the rack shaft positioned between them. The second pressing member urges the rack shaft toward the second pinion to maintain engagement between the second rack portion and the second pinion, particularly when assist torque is applied by the electric motor.

A characteristic feature of the device is that the first pressing member and the second pressing member are not formed with the same rigidity. Instead, the first pressing member has lower rigidity than the second pressing member. In other words, the first pressing member is more compliant or more easily deflected under load, while the second pressing member is comparatively stiffer. This difference in rigidity allows the support characteristics of the rack shaft to be optimized separately at the steering input side and at the assist motor side.

Because the first pressing member has lower rigidity, it can absorb or moderate small displacements, impacts, and vibrations transmitted through the rack shaft to the steering wheel. This can improve steering feel by reducing harshness, rattling, or excessive reaction force perceived by the driver. The more compliant support at the first pinion also helps maintain smooth mechanical engagement during manual steering operation.

On the other hand, the second pressing member has higher rigidity, which provides firm support for the rack shaft at the assist pinion. This is advantageous because the second pinion receives drive force from the electric assist motor and may be subjected to higher or rapidly changing loads. The increased rigidity helps maintain accurate meshing between the second pinion and the rack shaft, improving transmission efficiency of the assist force and contributing to stable assist performance.

By setting the rigidity of the first pressing member lower than that of the second pressing member, the steering device can provide both a comfortable steering feel at the steering wheel and reliable assist-force transmission from the motor. The arrangement therefore enables the rack shaft to be supported in a manner suited to the different functions of the two pinions: the first pinion primarily transmits the driver’s steering input, while the second pinion primarily transmits motor-generated assist force. As a result, the dual-pinion electric power steering device can achieve improved steering comfort, reduced vibration transmission, stable rack-and-pinion engagement, and enhanced electric assist performance.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in the English language, yet it plays a very important role. It is called the definite article because it points to something specific. When we say “the book,” “the sun,” or “the answer,” we are not talking about just any book, sun, or answer—we are referring to something known or particular.

This simple word helps bring clarity to communication. Without “the,” sentences can feel incomplete or confusing. For example, “I saw dog” sounds unnatural, but “I saw the dog” tells us that the speaker is referring to a specific dog. In this way, “the” helps connect ideas and gives meaning to the nouns around it.

Although it may seem ordinary, “the” is one of the most commonly used words in English. Its strength lies in its simplicity. It shows that even the smallest words can have a big impact on how we understand language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise patent-style abstract for a dual-pinion electric power steering device where the rack-side pressing member for the steering pinion is less rigid than the pressing member for the assist motor pinion.
counterfactuals.output: An electric power steering device includes a rack shaft, a steering pinion meshed with the rack shaft, and an assist pinion driven by an electric motor and meshed with the rack shaft at a position spaced from the steering pinion. A first rack-side pressing member urges the rack shaft toward the steering pinion, and a second rack-side pressing member urges the rack shaft toward the assist pinion. The first pressing member has a lower rigidity than the second pressing member. Accordingly, tooth engagement at the steering pinion is allowed to flexibly follow rack displacement to suppress rattling and steering vibration, while the assist pinion is supported with higher rigidity to efficiently transmit motor assist force.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Japanese-patent-style English abstract for an electric power steering device in which the rack guide opposite the manual steering pinion is softer than the rack guide opposite the motor-driven assist pinion.
counterfactuals.output:
PROBLEM TO BE SOLVED: To provide an electric power steering device capable of suppressing deterioration of steering feeling while ensuring stable meshing between a rack shaft and a motor-driven assist pinion.

SOLUTION: An electric power steering device includes a rack shaft having rack teeth, a manual steering pinion meshed with the rack shaft and rotated in accordance with operation of a steering wheel, a motor-driven assist pinion meshed with the rack shaft and driven by an electric motor, a first rack guide disposed opposite the manual steering pinion with the rack shaft interposed therebetween, and a second rack guide disposed opposite the motor-driven assist pinion with the rack shaft interposed therebetween. The first rack guide is configured to support the rack shaft with a lower rigidity than the second rack guide. Accordingly, impact and vibration transmitted from the rack shaft to the steering wheel through the manual steering pinion are reduced, while tooth separation and rattling at the motor-driven assist pinion are suppressed by the higher rigidity of the second rack guide. Thereby, both improved steering feel and reliable assist force transmission can be achieved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a technical description of a dual-pinion electric power steering mechanism: steering force is transmitted to a first pinion, motor torque to a second pinion, each meshes with rack teeth on a rack shaft, and separate pressing members bias the rack toward each pinion with the first being less rigid.
counterfactuals.output:
A dual-pinion electric power steering (EPS) mechanism includes a rack shaft provided with rack teeth and two pinions arranged to mesh with the rack teeth at axially spaced positions.

A steering input system transmits driver steering force from a steering wheel through a steering shaft to a first pinion. The first pinion meshes with the rack teeth of the rack shaft so that rotation of the steering shaft is converted into axial movement of the rack shaft.

An electric assist system includes an electric motor and a transmission mechanism, such as a reduction gear, for transmitting motor torque to a second pinion. The second pinion also meshes with the rack teeth of the rack shaft. Rotation of the second pinion applies assist force to the rack shaft in the axial direction, thereby assisting the steering force applied through the first pinion.

The rack shaft is supported in a housing and is biased toward the first and second pinions by separate rack pressing members. A first pressing member is disposed opposite the first pinion and urges the rack shaft toward the first pinion to maintain meshing engagement between the first pinion and the rack teeth. A second pressing member is disposed opposite the second pinion and urges the rack shaft toward the second pinion to maintain meshing engagement between the second pinion and the rack teeth.

The first pressing member has a lower rigidity than the second pressing member. As a result, the rack support at the driver-input pinion side is more compliant, allowing slight displacement of the rack shaft under steering input and road-load variations. This compliance can reduce gear rattle, tooth impact, and steering vibration transmitted to the steering wheel. The second pressing member, being more rigid, provides firmer support at the motor-assist pinion side, helping maintain stable gear engagement and efficient transmission of motor assist torque to the rack shaft.

Thus, the mechanism separately optimizes the rack support characteristics at the manual steering-force input side and at the electric assist-force input side. The less rigid first pressing member improves steering feel and noise/vibration performance, while the more rigid second pressing member improves assist torque transmission and rack positioning accuracy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
